passage: Four nights before her statistics exam in Lisbon, Beatriz was living on black tea and three hours of sleep. When Lindiwe knocked to borrow her lecture notes, Beatriz shouted, "Can't anyone do their own work?" and shut the door. An hour later, in the same fog, she emailed her group saying she was leaving the project and would do it alone. Then she fell asleep on her desk. She woke at noon, ate soup, and read her own email with a sinking stomach. She walked to Lindiwe's room with the notes and a packet of biscuits. "I was horrible. I'm sorry." Lindiwe took the biscuits. "You looked like a ghost. Sit down." That afternoon Beatriz asked the group if she could come back.

qa.q: What was Beatriz living on four nights before her exam?
qa.a: She was living on black tea and three hours of sleep.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling when she read her own email after waking?
qa.a: She felt a sinking dread and regret, realising the tired, rash decision to quit the group was a mistake.

qa.q: What turning point let Beatriz repair things?
qa.a: Sleeping and eating soup cleared her head, and she chose to apologise to Lindiwe and ask the group to take her back instead of defending her tired choices.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see Beatriz's outburst?
qa.a: Lindiwe noticed Beatriz looked like a ghost, so Lindiwe reads the shouting as exhaustion and forgives Beatriz easily.

passage: The hostel corridor smelled of instant coffee and fear the week before semester exams. Jasleen had slept four hours in two days and eaten mostly tea and biscuits. When her roommate Alka switched on the tube light at midnight, Jasleen snapped, "Are you trying to make me fail?" Alka switched it off without a word and studied with a torch. At two, Jasleen decided to skip the practical exam and cram theory instead. At breakfast in the mess, over a proper plate of poha, she heard herself explain the plan to a senior and felt sick at how silly it sounded. She went back to the room. "Alka, I'm sorry about last night. I wasn't thinking straight." Alka shrugged and smiled. "You weren't sleeping straight either."

qa.q: What had Jasleen eaten mostly in the two days before?
qa.a: Mostly tea and biscuits.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen feel sick when she explained her plan at breakfast?
qa.a: Now that she had eaten, she could hear how rash and silly skipping the practical was, and she regretted the idea.

qa.q: Which choice helped Jasleen most after the bad night?
qa.a: Eating a proper breakfast gave her a clearer head, which let her see the bad plan and choose to apologise to Alka.

qa.q: What was the night like for Alka?
qa.a: Alka was snapped at for switching on a light and had to study with a torch, but Alka understood that Jasleen's tiredness caused it and forgave Jasleen with a joke.

grounding: In a hostel before exams, a tired and hungry student snaps at her roommate and plans a rash choice, then sees it clearly after eating.

I'm Dhruv, Manoj's roommate. Exam week, he was a different person. He lived on tea from the hostel canteen and slept on the desk, not the bed. When Aman borrowed his charger, Manoj yelled at him. Aman is his closest friend.
On Wednesday at four in the morning, I woke to find Manoj typing fast. He said, "I'm emailing the department. I'm dropping the semester. I'm done." His eyes were red. I didn't know what to say, so I just said, "Maybe sleep first?" He sent it anyway.
Then he slept twelve hours. When he woke, I gave him the parathas my mother had packed. He ate four, went pale, and opened his laptop. He wrote to the department asking them to ignore his email. Then he went to find Aman.
I don't know everything he was feeling. But the Manoj who ate breakfast was not the Manoj who typed at four.

qa.q: What did Dhruv give Manoj when he woke?
qa.a: The parathas Dhruv's mother had packed.

qa.q: What might Manoj have felt when he went pale after eating?
qa.a: He probably felt shock and regret as he realised, rested and fed, what he had done while exhausted at four in the morning.

qa.q: Where was the turning point, and what did Manoj choose to do after it?
qa.a: After sleeping and eating he saw his rash email clearly, so he wrote to ask the department to ignore it and went to make up with Aman.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt when Manoj yelled at him over a charger?
qa.a: Aman probably felt hurt and shocked, since he is Manoj's closest friend and only borrowed a charger.

Dear Vidya,
I owe you an apology, and I'm writing because I'm a coward on the phone.
Last week, in the middle of exams, I'd slept maybe eight hours across three nights and lived on tea and biscuits. When you asked me to check your notes, I told you to stop being so needy. That was cruel. You didn't deserve it.

I slept twelve hours on Saturday and ate a real meal, and I woke up horrified at both.
I'm sorry. Can I buy you dosa and try to be a human again?
Samir

Arnab, you asked on this podcast about my worst exam week. I'm Shankar, and it's this.
Final year, second semester. Three all-nighters. I lived on cutting chai and those orange biscuits. By Wednesday my hands shook.
My roommate asked if I'd seen his charger. I yelled at him, full volume. Over a charger.
Then at 4 am, I read one rude message in our project group and I quit. Wrote a long message, left the group, told them to finish it without me.
Thursday I slept. Friday I ate a proper meal. Saturday I read what I'd written and wanted to disappear.
I had to go back and ask to rejoin. They let me, but it cost me.
What I learned is simple: tired and hungry me is not the real me. And the real me has to protect him.

qa.q: What did Shankar live on during the exam week?
qa.a: Cutting chai and orange biscuits.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling on Saturday reading the message?
qa.a: Shankar felt ashamed and full of regret, wanting to disappear.

qa.q: What could Shankar do before making decisions in a week like that?
qa.a: Eat and sleep first, and wait before sending messages or quitting, since a rested mind judges and forgives better.

qa.q: How might the roommate have felt when Shankar yelled about the charger?
qa.a: He probably felt shocked and hurt by a big reaction to a small question.

Monday. Jyoti's third all-nighter. Six cups of tea, a packet of biscuits, no dinner. When Mridul knocked to ask about lunch, she said, "Can you not see I'm busy?" and shut the door.
Tuesday. At 5 am, she read her project draft, decided it was all rubbish, and deleted two weeks of work. It felt brave at the time.
Thursday. The exam was over. She'd slept eleven hours and eaten rice and dal at Mridul's. She sat staring at the empty folder on her laptop, sick with regret.
She found Mridul in the corridor. "I was awful on Monday. I'm sorry."
Mridul shrugged. "You looked like a zombie. I figured it wasn't you."
Jyoti laughed shakily. "It wasn't. It was the tea."

qa.q: How many cups of tea did Jyoti drink on Monday?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling while staring at the empty folder?
qa.a: She felt sick with regret about deleting two weeks of work in an exhausted moment.

qa.q: What could Jyoti have done at 5 am on Tuesday instead of deleting the work?
qa.a: She could have saved it and slept, deciding about the draft after rest and a meal.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Jyoti's behaviour on Monday?
qa.a: Mridul sees it as exhaustion, not her real self, and forgives easily.

"Indu, you are studying all night again? Sit, let your Nani tell you something.
When I was twenty, I, Ganga, was doing my BSc in Madras. Before the final exams I lived on hostel tea and two hours of sleep. I thought it made me brave.
The night before chemistry, my best friend Rukmini asked to borrow my notes. I shouted at her in front of the whole corridor, called her lazy. Then I sold my good fountain pen to a senior for nothing, just to be rid of it, because it was leaking.
I passed, barely. But Rukmini didn't speak to me for a month, and I cried over that pen.
Afterwards I learned: after a meal and a real sleep, I could not even understand why I'd been so cruel. A rested mind forgives. A starving one bites."

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel after the exams about what she had done?
qa.a: She felt regret and sorrow, crying over the pen and hurt that Rukmini didn't speak to her for a month.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could Ganga have made differently the night before chemistry?
qa.a: She could have eaten and slept instead of pushing on with tea, so she would not have snapped at Rukmini or made a rash choice with the pen.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt when Ganga shouted at her in the corridor?
qa.a: Rukmini was probably hurt and humiliated, being called lazy in front of everyone just for asking to borrow notes.

Two days before his law exams, Madhav had not slept a full night in a week. He sat in his rented room in Andheri with cold tea and a packet of rusks, the ceiling fan clicking.
His friend Anand messaged: "Coming to study together? I'll bring food."
Madhav typed back: "Stop treating me like a child. I don't need you."
He stared at it after sending. At midnight, restless, he signed up for a costly weekend course online without reading the details.
The next afternoon he woke at three, ate, and saw both screens clearly. His stomach dropped. He called Anand. "I'm sorry. I was running on nothing."
Anand laughed, a bit hurt. "You bite when you're hungry. Come, there's dal."

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he saw both screens clearly the next afternoon?
qa.a: His stomach dropped with regret and shame at the harsh message and the rash course signup.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhav before his next big exam?
qa.a: Keep regular meals and sleep, accept offers like Anand's, and wait until rested before making decisions or sending sharp replies.

qa.q: How does Anand see Madhav's harsh message after the apology?
qa.a: Anand is a bit hurt but forgiving, understanding that Madhav 'bites when he's hungry', and still offers dal.

I have been watching Gurpreet (2nd year) this week. She has been awake most nights, living on tea and instant noodles. On Tuesday she shouted at her roommate Yamini over a light switch. On Wednesday she told me she was going to 'just drop out, what's the point', which surprised me, as she is a strong student. I sent her to bed at eleven and asked Yamini to make sure she came to breakfast. This morning, after sleep and a proper meal, she came to my office on her own. She said, 'I didn't mean the drop-out thing. I was so tired I couldn't think.' She has also apologised to Yamini. Next step: I'll put up a notice about lights-out in exam week.

Mrs Kaur, warden
